title: Cyllenian Hermes, guide of souls
greek: Ἑρμῆς Κυλλήνιος (Hermēs Kyllēnios); ψυχοπομπός (psychopompos)
short: Hermes 'of Cyllene', the Arcadian mountain of his birth, leads the suitors' souls to Hades: his only appearance in Homer as psychopompos, 'escort of souls'.
body: Mount Cyllene in Arcadia was Hermes' birthplace (Homeric Hymn to Hermes 1-3), and Kyllēnios is a regular epithet in the Homeric Hymns. Monro reports Aristarchus' observation that the epithet is post-Homeric, and also that the role of escorting souls is 'nowhere else mentioned in Homer', although deaths are described countless times; elsewhere souls simply go down under the earth. Monro adds that the contracted form Hermēs in 24.1 is post-Homeric, while the archaic 'Hermeias the helper' (akakēta) appears at 24.10. These observations were among Aristarchus' reasons for rejecting 24.1-204. The guide-of-souls role became central in later Greek religion; Hermes Psychopompos became familiar in later Greek art and literature.

title: Hermes' golden wand (rhabdos)
greek: ῥάβδος χρυσείη (rhabdos chryseiē)
short: With his golden wand Hermes charms the eyes of men to sleep or wakes them, and with it he rouses and drives the souls of the dead.
body: The description of the wand repeats Il. 24.343-4 and Od. 5.47-8, where Hermes sets out on a mission for Zeus. The power to close and open eyes, to bring sleep and waking, fits a god who crosses boundaries, between sleep and waking and between life and death. Circe too has a wand (10.238, 10.293), with which she transforms men. Hermes' herald's staff (kērukeion) became in later art the caduceus with twin snakes; Homer's rhabdos is simply a magic gold rod. Here the wand 'stirs' the souls (kinēsas), and they follow 'gibbering', as the next simile describes.

title: Simile: the souls gibber like bats in a cave
greek: τρίζουσαι (trizousai); νυκτερίδες (nukterides)
short: The suitors' souls follow Hermes squeaking like bats in a cavern when one drops from the clinging cluster on the rock.
body: Trizō is used of thin, shrill sounds; Monro explains the perfect tetriguiai of 'the peculiar shrill note of the bat' sustained over time. In the Iliad the soul of Patroclus goes beneath the earth 'like smoke, gibbering' (tetriguia, Il. 23.100-1), so the sound of the dead is traditional. Monro explains hormathos as the 'chain' of bats clinging together, from which one drops off the rock. The simile captures the insubstantial, helpless and crowded state of the dead in Homeric belief, in which the psychē is a shadowy image (eidōlon) without strength or full consciousness. Shakespeare's 'the sheeted dead / Did squeak and gibber in the Roman streets' (Hamlet 1.1) belongs to the same tradition.

title: The way to Hades: Ocean, the White Rock, the Gates of the Sun, the Land of Dreams
greek: Λευκὰς πέτρη (Leukas petrē); Ἠελίοιο πύλαι (Ēelioio pulai); δῆμος ὀνείρων (dēmos oneirōn)
short: The souls pass the streams of Ocean, the White Rock, the gates of the Sun and the land of dreams, and reach the mead of asphodel where the dead dwell.
body: Monro comments that 'the White Rock is only mentioned here', that the Gates of the Sun belong to the idea of Hades lying in the darkness of the far west, where the sun enters at setting, and that the Land of Dreams is known from this passage only. He also notes that the route ignores the rule, stated by the shade of Patroclus (Il. 23.71-4) and implied by Elpenor (11.51-80), that the unburied cannot join the dead, an inconsistency Aristarchus raised. Strabo explains that the island of Leucas, once a peninsula of the mainland, took its later name from the white cliff Leucatas jutting into the sea (10.2.8). Gregory Nagy has connected the White Rock with the setting sun and with the mythical leap from the Leucadian cliff.

title: The 'Second Nekyia' (24.1-204) and its authenticity
greek: Νέκυια δευτέρα (Nekuia deutera)
short: The second scene among the dead, where Agamemnon and Achilles meet the suitors' souls, was rejected by Aristarchus and remains the most disputed part of the ending.
body: Monro summarises Aristarchus' objections as preserved in the scholia: Hermes as psychopompos and his epithet Kyllēnios are un-Homeric; the unburied suitors enter Hades; the dialogue of Achilles and Agamemnon is out of place (akairos), for the newcomers must wait until it is done; and the language shows late features. Ancient defenders replied point by point and called this the true 'descent' (katabasis), as opposed to the consultation of the dead in Book XI. Monro thinks the cumulative case 'can hardly be resisted' and that a second Hades scene is 'poetically speaking, a failure'. Many modern critics see instead a deliberate ending that weighs the three great heroes' fates: Achilles' glorious death and funeral, Agamemnon's murder at home, and Odysseus' triumph thanks to a faithful wife.

title: Achilles in the dust: a line from the Iliad
greek: κεῖσο μέγας μεγαλωστί, λελασμένος ἱπποσυνάων (keiso megas megalōsti, lelasmenos hipposunaōn)
short: Agamemnon describes Achilles' corpse 'lying mighty in thy mightiness in the whirl of dust, forgetful of thy horsemanship', words used in the Iliad of Hector's charioteer Cebriones.
body: In the Iliad the lines describe Cebriones, killed by Patroclus, around whose body Greeks and Trojans fight (Il. 16.775-6). Monro, following Sittl, observes that 'forgetful of horsemanship' is more appropriate there, said of a chariot-driver. The reuse fits Achilles' death, which the Iliad does not narrate: according to Proclus' summary of the Aethiopis, Achilles was killed by Paris and Apollo, Ajax carried the body to the ships while Odysseus held off the Trojans, and Thetis came with the Muses and her sisters to mourn. Agamemnon's speech thus supplies, from within the Odyssey, the ending of Achilles' story, including the storm that ended the fighting (24.41-2).

title: Thetis and the Nereids lament Achilles
greek: κοῦραι ἁλίοιο γέροντος (kourai halioio gerontos)
short: Thetis rises from the sea with the sea-nymphs; the Achaeans almost flee until Nestor explains, and the Nereids dress Achilles in immortal clothing.
body: The 'old man of the sea' here is Nereus, father of the fifty Nereids (Hesiod, Theogony 233-64); the title is also used of Proteus in Book IV. The scene expands Il. 18.35-69, where Thetis and her sisters lament Achilles while he still lives, as if already dead. Monro notes that this is the only place in the Odyssey where the word phobos ('flight, panic') occurs, and that Nestor's formula 'whose counsel had before appeared the best' is hardly apt here. Aristarchus objected that the Greeks were already at the ships (24.43); Monro answers that they rush to the ships to flee. Proclus' summary of the Aethiopis confirms that the lament by Thetis with the Muses and her sisters belonged to the cyclic tradition.

title: The nine Muses sing the dirge
greek: Μοῦσαι δ' ἐννέα πᾶσαι ἀμειβόμεναι ὀπὶ καλῇ θρήνεον (Mousai d' ennea pasai ameibomenai opi kalēi thrēneon)
short: The Muses lead the lament for Achilles in alternating song: the only place in Homer that gives the number of the Muses.
body: Monro reports Aristarchus' note that this is the only Homeric passage giving the Muses' number, and suggests that it 'may be the source of the later belief'; he adds that the words need only mean that nine in all took part in this lament. Hesiod's Theogony (76-9) names nine Muses, daughters of Zeus and Memory. The dirge (thrēnos) sung responsively, 'answering one another' (ameibomenai), matches the formal lament for Hector, where professional singers lead and the women respond (Il. 24.720-2). Monro notes the abrupt change to the singular 'the clear-toned Muse' (24.62). The Muses' presence makes Achilles' funeral a divine event, and also an image of the epic tradition mourning its greatest hero.

title: The funeral of Achilles
greek: ἑπτὰ καὶ δέκα... ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ δ' ἔδομεν πυρί (hepta kai deka... oktōkaidekatēi d' edomen puri)
short: Gods and men mourn Achilles for seventeen days and nights; on the eighteenth he is cremated with sheep, cattle, unguents and honey, and his bones are laid in unmixed wine.
body: The ritual follows the pattern of Homeric funerals: washing and anointing the body, laying it on a bier, cutting the hair, lament, cremation with animal victims, gathering the bones in wine and oil, an urn, a mound and games. Compare Patroclus' funeral (Il. 23.110-257) and Hector's, after nine days of mourning (Il. 24.784-804). Monro notes that Aristarchus asked how the body was preserved for so many days (the scholiast answers: by Thetis, as for Patroclus, Il. 19.38-9), and that the honey may be a trace of embalming. Warriors marching around the pyre in armour (24.68-70) recall the Myrmidons' ritual for Patroclus (Il. 23.13-14). The scale of the funeral expresses Achilles' honour (timē).

title: The golden amphora, gift of Dionysus
greek: χρύσεος ἀμφιφορεύς (chryseos amphiphoreus); Διωνύσοιο δῶρον (Diōnusoio dōron)
short: Thetis provides a two-handled golden urn, made by Hephaestus and given by Dionysus, in which the bones of Achilles and Patroclus are mingled.
body: In the Iliad the shade of Patroclus asks that his bones and Achilles' should lie together in one vessel, the golden amphiphoreus Thetis gave (Il. 23.91-2); his bones were first placed in a golden bowl (phialē, Il. 23.243, 253), as Monro notes. The Odyssey fulfils the request, while Antilochus' bones lie apart. Dionysus as giver is unusual in Homer, where he is a minor figure, but the story was known in art: on the François Vase Dionysus carries an amphora to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, which later tradition identified with this urn. Gregory Nagy reads the gold vessel, a gift of the god of wine and of renewal, as a sign of the heroes' immortalisation in cult.

title: The tomb of Achilles on the Hellespont
greek: τύμβος... ἀκτῇ ἔπι προὐχούσῃ, ἐπὶ πλατεῖ Ἑλλησπόντῳ (tumbos... aktēi epi prouchousēi, epi platei Hellēspontōi); τηλεφανής (tēlephanēs)
short: The army heaps a great mound on a jutting headland over the Hellespont, 'shining from afar' to sailors of the present and the future.
body: The burial mound (tumbos) visible from the sea is the physical form of kleos, fame that outlives the hero. Hector imagines the tomb of a man he kills, on the Hellespont, which a sailor will see and say 'this is the mound of a man who died long ago, whom glorious Hector killed' (Il. 7.86-91). In historical times tumuli at Sigeum on the Troad coast were identified as the tombs of Achilles, Patroclus and Antilochus, and Strabo reports that the people of Ilium sacrificed to all of them (13.1.32); Monro notes that later the three heroes had separate mounds. Nagy stresses the epithet tēlephanēs, 'seen from far', and reads the tomb as a beacon of safety for sailors. Monro discusses hieros stratos, 'the mighty host', at 24.81.

title: Funeral games with prizes from the gods
greek: περικαλλέ' ἄεθλα... ἐν ἀγῶνι (perikalle' aethla... en agōni)
short: Thetis obtains splendid prizes from the gods and sets them out for the best of the Achaeans in games for her son.
body: Athletic contests at a great man's funeral were a regular institution: Book XXIII of the Iliad describes Achilles' games for Patroclus, Nestor remembers competing in the games for Amarynceus (Il. 23.629-42), and Hesiod won a tripod at the games for Amphidamas (Works and Days 654-7). Proclus' summary of the Aethiopis records the games for Achilles, followed by the quarrel of Ajax and Odysseus over his arms, which Odysseus recalled with regret in the underworld (11.543-62). Monro discusses the grammatical difficulty of hote ken... zōnnuntai (24.88-9). Agamemnon's remark that Achilles was 'very dear to the gods' (24.92) explains the divine prizes, and leads into the theme of undying fame.

title: Kleos: Achilles' undying fame and Agamemnon's bitterness
greek: οὐδὲ θανὼν ὄνομ' ὤλεσας, ἀλλά τοι αἰεὶ πάντας ἐπ' ἀνθρώπους κλέος ἔσσεται ἐσθλόν (oude thanōn onom' ōlesas, alla toi aiei pantas ep' anthrōpous kleos essetai esthlon)
short: Agamemnon tells Achilles that even in death his name lives and his kleos will be noble among all men forever, while his own return brought only a shameful death.
body: Kleos, literally 'what is heard', is the fame carried by song, the reward for which Achilles chose a short life (Il. 9.410-16). In Book XI Achilles' shade had rejected that bargain, preferring to be a hired labourer on earth than king of the dead (11.488-91); here, in the second underworld scene, Agamemnon reaffirms the value of his glory. Monro explains ti tode ēdos as 'how is it now a pleasure?' and notes that only here and in Book XI is Clytemnestra said to have joined in the murder. Agamemnon's contrast of three fates prepares his praise of Penelope, whose kleos will be sung by the gods, and his curse on Clytemnestra, whose song will be hateful (24.196-202).

title: Amphimedon, Agamemnon's guest-friend
greek: Ἀμφιμέδων, παῖς Μελανῆος (Amphimedōn, pais Melanēos)
short: Agamemnon recognises among the dead suitors Amphimedon son of Melaneus, who had been his host in Ithaca when he came to recruit Odysseus for Troy.
body: Amphimedon was killed by Telemachus (22.284) after wounding him in the wrist (22.277-8). The tie of guest-friendship (xenia) explains why he speaks for the suitors: Agamemnon calls himself 'a friend of your house'. Monro explains 'host in Ithaca, his home', comparing Il. 6.224-5, where Diomedes is Glaucus' guest-friend in Argos. Agamemnon recalls that it took a whole month (Monro: 'just a good month') to persuade Odysseus to go to Troy (24.115-19), a hint of the story, told in the Cypria, that Odysseus feigned madness to avoid the war. Agamemnon's guesses about how so many young men died together, by shipwreck or raiding, are the deaths of the epic world (24.109-13 = 11.399-403).

anchor: in his great cunning he bade
title: Amphimedon's version: was Penelope in the plot?
greek: αὐτὰρ ὁ ἣν ἄλοχον πολυκερδείῃσιν ἄνωγε (autar ho hēn alochon polukerdeiēisin anōge)
short: The dead suitor retells the web and the slaughter, but claims Odysseus 'in his great cunning' told his wife to set the contest, which the poem never said.
body: In Books XIX-XXI Penelope proposes the contest on her own initiative (19.570-81), and Odysseus merely urges her to hold it. Amphimedon's account also makes the end of the web coincide with Odysseus' return (24.147-50). Monro reports that these discrepancies have been 'much insisted upon by modern scholars, as pointing to the existence of a different form of the story', perhaps one in which husband and wife plotted together after an earlier recognition. He himself thinks no conclusion can be founded on them, since a dead suitor's partial knowledge naturally produces such inaccuracies. The web story repeats 2.93-110 and 19.138-56. Amphimedon complains that their bodies lie unburied, unwashed and unlamented, 'for that is the due (geras) of the dead' (24.186-90).

title: 'Happy son of Laertes': Penelope's aretē and her song
greek: ὄλβιε Λαέρταο πάϊ... σὺν μεγάλῃ ἀρετῇ ἐκτήσω ἄκοιτιν (olbie Laertao pai... sun megalēi aretēi ektēsō akoitin)
short: Agamemnon blesses Odysseus for winning a wife of great excellence: the gods will make a delightful song for constant Penelope, and the fame of her virtue will never perish.
body: Olbios means blessed with good fortune and prosperity, the opposite of Agamemnon's own fate. Aretē here is 'excellence' in the full sense: Monro takes sun megalēi aretēi as 'with a dower of noble gifts', including all her qualities of character and person. The lines raise an ambiguity: in 'his fame (kleos) shall never perish, of her virtue', the pronoun hoi could refer to Odysseus (his fame, won by her virtue) or to Penelope; many readers take it as Penelope's own kleos, which would make her the only woman in Homer promised epic fame for her own deeds. The 'song' (aoidē) the gods will make for 'prudent Penelope' (echephroni Pēnelopeiēi; Monro on 24.198) may be read as the Odyssey itself.

title: Clytemnestra, the counter-example
greek: Τυνδαρέου κούρη (Tyndareou kourē); στυγερὴ ἀοιδή (stugerē aoidē)
short: Unlike Penelope, Clytemnestra, daughter of Tyndareus, plotted evil and killed her husband; the song about her will be hateful and will shame all women.
body: The story of Agamemnon's murder by Aegisthus and Clytemnestra and Orestes' revenge runs through the Odyssey as a model and warning: Zeus cites it in the first divine council (1.29-43), Nestor and Menelaus tell it to Telemachus (3.254-312, 4.512-37), and Agamemnon's shade tells his own version (11.405-56). Monro notes that only here and in Book XI is Clytemnestra said to have taken part in the killing; elsewhere it is Aegisthus' deed. The opposition of the faithful and the murderous wife closes the poem's long comparison between the two homecomings. Agamemnon's bitter conclusion, that Clytemnestra's infamy falls 'even on the woman who acts rightly', echoes his advice to Odysseus in Book XI not to trust even Penelope fully (11.441-56).

title: The old Sicilian woman on Laertes' farm
greek: γυνὴ Σικελὴ γρηΰς (gunē Sikelē grēus)
short: Laertes is cared for by an old Sicilian slave woman, the wife of Dolius: one of only a handful of references in Homer to the Sikels of Sicily.
body: The Sikeloi, who gave their name to Sicily, appear earlier as people to whom the suitors propose selling Odysseus and Theoclymenus as slaves (20.382-3), so a 'Sicilian woman' was probably bought as a slave. Monro, referring to that passage, notes that the Sikels are known as buyers of slaves. Thucydides distinguishes the Sicels from the Sicanians, after whom the island was earlier called Sicania (6.2.2); the false name Odysseus gives Laertes includes a voyage 'from Sicania' (24.307), which Monro notes is 'nowhere else mentioned in Homer'. Monro also describes the farm's arrangement: an oikos or main room, like the megaron of a palace, surrounded by sheds (klisia) for the bondsmen. The farm is land Laertes won by his own labour (24.205-7).

title: Laertes in his vineyard
greek: κνημῖδες βόειαι (knēmides boeiai); χειρῖδες (cheirides); κυνέη αἰγείη (kuneē aigeiē)
short: Odysseus finds his father alone, digging round a plant in a patched tunic, with leather gaiters against scratches, gloves against thorns and a goatskin cap, 'nursing his grief'.
body: Monro explains that the knēmides are 'greaves' or 'gaiters', the same word as for the bronze greaves of warriors, and that cheirides is formed from cheir, 'hand', on the analogy of knēmides. The phrase penthos aexōn, 'cherishing his sorrow', explains the deliberate roughness of his dress, a form of mourning. Laertes' withdrawal was described by Athena-Mentes (1.189-93) and by the shade of Anticleia, who said he sleeps in winter among the slaves in ashes by the fire and in summer on leaves in the vineyard (11.187-96). The picture of the old king as a working gardener is unique in Homer, and its realism, which Monro's notes repeatedly mark as unusual in language, has been both admired and suspected.

title: Odysseus tests his father 'with mocking words'
greek: πρῶτον κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσιν πειρηθῆναι (prōton kertomiois epeessin peirēthēnai)
short: Instead of embracing his grieving father, Odysseus decides to test him first with teasing, provocative speech and a false story.
body: Kertomios describes taunting or provocative words. The decision has puzzled readers, since Laertes is no threat, and some find the scene needlessly cruel; others see Odysseus' ingrained habit of testing before revealing, which Athena herself praised as his chief characteristic (13.330-6), and a way of drawing out Laertes' grief so that the recognition is complete. Monro shows that the deliberation (24.235-40) is modelled on 10.151-4 and finds features of late composition, notably the construction with the infinitive and the irregular metre of epeessin in 24.240, 'the only real exception' to a rule of the Homeric hexameter. Odysseus' praise of the garden and his suggestion that Laertes looks like a king, not a slave (24.244-55), are a sharp mixture of flattery and reproach.

title: Odysseus' last lie: Eperitus of Alybas
greek: Ἀλύβας (Alybas); Ἀφείδας (Apheidas); Πολυπημονίδης (Polypēmonidēs); Ἐπήριτος (Epēritos)
short: Odysseus claims to be Eperitus, son of Apheidas son of Polypemon, from Alybas, driven from Sicania, and says he entertained Odysseus five years ago.
body: This is the last of Odysseus' false tales, and its names are 'speaking'. Monro suggests that Polypēmonidēs may point to the 'much-suffering' family of Laertes, or to riches (polupamōn, 'possessing much'); Apheidas would mean 'Unsparing', and Epēritos, from eris, 'strife', may allude to the meaning of the name Odysseus, which his grandfather Autolycus explained from odussomai, 'to be angry with' (19.406-9). Alybas is otherwise unknown; ancient commentators placed it variously. The false tale of having hosted Odysseus and given him lavish guest-gifts touches Laertes at his deepest point, the expected return of xenia, and his response, pouring dust on his head, makes Odysseus break down.

title: The orchard as a token of identity
greek: ὄγχνας μοι δῶκας τρισκαίδεκα καὶ δέκα μηλέας, συκέας τεσσαράκοντ' (onchnas moi dōkas triskaideka kai deka mēleas, sukeas tessarakont')
short: Asked for a sign, Odysseus shows the scar and lists the trees his father gave him as a child: thirteen pears, ten apples, forty figs, fifty vine-rows.
body: The two signs complement each other. The scar recalls the boy's journey to his grandfather Autolycus; the trees recall the small boy following his father through the orchard asking the name of each one. Like the bed of Book XXIII, the sign is rooted, living and known only within the family, and it concerns inheritance: the boy's own share of the land. Monro notes difficulties in the text, including the non-Homeric form ēēn (24.343) and an awkward optative (24.344). Laertes' 'knees and heart were loosened' (24.345), the formula used of Penelope's recognition (23.205); he faints, and on reviving his first words are a theodicy: the gods still rule on Olympus if the suitors have paid for their insolence (24.351-2).

title: Nericus and the Cephallenians
greek: Νήρικος (Nērikos); Κεφαλλῆνες (Kephallēnes)
short: Rejuvenated by Athena, Laertes wishes he had fought the suitors with the strength he had when he took Nericus 'on the shore of the mainland' as lord of the Cephallenians.
body: The Cephallenians are the people of Odysseus' realm in the Catalogue of Ships (Il. 2.631), and Monro notes the name's use for the whole kingdom (24.355, 378). Strabo identifies Nericus with a town on Leucas, which in early times was a peninsula of the mainland (Acarnania), and says the Corinthians later moved the settlement and renamed it Leucas (10.2.8); he also warns against confusing Nericus with Mount Neritus on Ithaca. Laertes' memory of his youthful conquest prepares his last exploit, the killing of Eupeithes. Monro notes that his transfiguration in the bath (24.367-70) is 'an awkward imitation' of Athena's similar changes to Odysseus.

title: Ossa, Rumour personified
greek: Ὄσσα δ' ἄρ' ἄγγελος (Ossa d' ar' angelos)
short: Rumour (Ossa), the messenger, races through the city telling of the suitors' death, and the families gather to collect their dead.
body: Ossa, related to the root of 'voice', means a voice or rumour of unknown origin, often thought of as divine. In the Iliad Ossa 'blazed among them, the messenger of Zeus' to gather the army (Il. 2.93-4). Its personification here as angelos ('messenger') anticipates Virgil's monstrous Fama, who runs through Libya spreading word of Dido and Aeneas (Aeneid 4.173-97). The spread of the news, which Odysseus foresaw at sunrise (23.362-3), makes the blood-feud inevitable. The families bury their dead and send those from other islands home by ship (24.417-19), giving the suitors at last the funeral rites Amphimedon lamented, and then meet in assembly.

title: Eupeithes, father of Antinous
greek: Εὐπείθης (Eupeithēs); Εὐπείθει πείθοντο (Eupeithei peithonto)
short: Antinous' father calls the Ithacans to avenge their sons; more than half follow him, ignoring the warnings of Medon and the seer Halitherses.
body: The name Eupeithēs means 'persuasive' or 'easily obeyed', and Monro points out the play in 24.465, Eupeithei peithonto, 'they obeyed Eupeithes'. Odysseus had once protected Eupeithes from the anger of the people when he fled to Ithaca after raiding the Thesprotians (16.424-30), so his son's insolence was already a betrayal of a benefactor. His speech states the heroic law of vengeance: it would be a disgrace for the future 'if we shall not take vengeance on the slayers of our sons and brothers' (24.433-5). Medon's report of a god fighting beside Odysseus and Halitherses' reminder of the people's own failure to restrain their sons (24.443-62) offer the opposing view. Monro notes several non-Homeric forms in the passage.

anchor: let them swear a solemn oath
title: Zeus' settlement: oath and 'forgetting'
greek: ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες... ἔκλησιν θέωμεν (horkia pista tamontes... eklēsin theōmen)
short: Zeus proposes that Odysseus, avenged, should be king for ever under sworn oaths, while the gods impose a 'forgetting' of the killings so both sides may be friends.
body: Horkia pista tamnein, literally 'to cut trusty oaths', refers to the sacrifice of victims by which treaties were sealed (Il. 3.245-301). Eklēsis, 'forgetting', occurs only here; Monro glosses it as 'an amnesty', and paraphrases Zeus: Athena caused the killing and must now meet the danger of the consequent blood-feud, but he proposes a treaty with amnesty for the blood shed. Monro observes that 24.479-80 repeat 5.23-4, where the sense is simpler, and that the abrupt change of scene to Olympus 'would hardly be possible with Homer'. The idea of an officially imposed forgetting has a famous historical parallel in the Athenian amnesty of 403 BC after the rule of the Thirty, when citizens swore 'not to remember wrongs' (mē mnēsikakein).

anchor: my son and my son's son
title: Three generations in arms
greek: υἱός θ' υἱωνός τ' ἀρετῆς πέρι δῆριν ἔχουσιν (huios th' huiōnos t' aretēs peri dērin echousin)
short: Laertes rejoices that his son and grandson are competing in courage; then, at Athena's prompting, he hurls his spear and kills Eupeithes.
body: Odysseus tells Telemachus not to shame 'the house of your fathers' (24.508), Telemachus promises to bring no disgrace, and Laertes exclaims at the rivalry of son and grandson in aretē, 'excellence, valour'. Monro finds Odysseus' exhortation 'out of place after the battle with the Suitors'. Athena addresses Laertes as 'son of Arceisius', naming the third generation back: the line of single sons, 'for Zeus made our race one of only sons' (16.117-20), is now complete and united. Laertes' spear-cast through Eupeithes' helmet is his one heroic deed in the poem, granted by the goddess; it closes the circle opened by the rusting shield of his youth (22.184-6) and kills the father of the first suitor Odysseus slew.

title: The final covenant and the ending of the Odyssey
greek: ὅρκια δ' αὖ κατόπισθε μετ' ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔθηκε Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη... Μέντορι εἰδομένη (horkia d' au katopisthe met' amphoteroisin ethēke Pallas Athēnaiē... Mentori eidomenē)
short: Athena halts the fighting with a shout, Zeus' thunderbolt stops Odysseus' pursuit, and the goddess, in the likeness of Mentor, establishes oaths of peace between the two sides.
body: The poem ends as it began, with Athena in disguise among the people of Ithaca: she came as Mentes in Book I and as Mentor in Book II, and the last word of the poem is 'voice' in the formula 'like Mentor in form and in voice'. Odysseus swoops 'like an eagle of lofty flight' (24.538), and only Zeus' bolt falling at Athena's feet checks him. Critics who accept Aristarchus' 'end' at 23.296 find the last scene hurried; Monro calls the easy victory 'full of improbabilities, which the poet does not attempt to soften or disguise, as Homer would assuredly have done', and marks late linguistic features in 24.534-5. Defenders argue that without it the blood-feud announced at 23.118-22 would be left unresolved, and that a peace imposed by the gods is a fitting close to a poem about the restoration of order.
